title: Broncos Legend Tom Jackson, ESPN ‘Sunday NFL Countdown’ Analyst, Dies at 75 – AP News
body:
Denver’s legendary “Orange Crush” linebacker and longtime ESPN analyst Tom Jackson died on Friday at the age of 75, the family confirmed to the network. The news was deliberately held back until the live broadcast of ESPN’s “Sunday NFL Countdown,” where co‑host Ryan Clark delivered the somber announcement to a nationwide audience. Jackson’s passing marks the end of an era for both the Broncos’ storied defense of the late 1970s and the voice that has guided football fans through three decades of NFL coverage.

Jackson’s football career began in the gritty streets of Detroit, where his tenacity earned him a scholarship to the University of Louisville. Drafted by Denver in the second round of the 1973 NFL Draft, he quickly became the emotional engine of the Broncos’ defense. Nicknamed “the Fireball,” his relentless pursuit of quarterbacks helped shape the “Orange Crush” unit that vaulted the franchise to its first Super Bowl appearance in 1977 and a championship victory in 1998. Over 12 seasons, Jackson amassed 11 interceptions, 13 sacks, and a reputation for delivering hard‑hitting, high‑energy play that set the tone for the entire team.

After hanging up his cleats in 1985, Jackson transitioned seamlessly into broadcasting, joining ESPN in 1994 as a color commentator for “Sunday NFL Countdown.” His distinctive gravelly voice, candid opinions, and ability to break down complex schemes made him a fan favorite and a trusted analyst for coaches, players, and casual viewers alike. Over the past three decades, he has covered every major NFL milestone—from the rise of the New England Patriots dynasty to the recent surge of mobile quarterback offenses—offering insights that blend his on‑field experience with a storyteller’s flair.

Beyond the mic, Jackson’s influence extended into philanthropy and mentorship. He founded the Tom Jackson Youth Football Academy in Denver, a program designed to provide underprivileged kids with coaching, academic support, and life‑skills training. Former NFL star and current coach Sean Payton credits the academy for shaping his early love of the game, while former Broncos teammates recall Jackson’s habit of visiting hospitals and community centers during off‑season weeks. His charitable work earned him the NFL’s Walter Payton Man of the Year nomination in 1992, underscoring a commitment to service that matched his on‑field intensity.

The Broncos organization and the broader NFL community responded quickly with tributes. Broncos owner Stan Kroenke released a statement describing Jackson as “the heart and soul of our defense and a timeless ambassador for the sport.” Current head coach Sean Payton, who worked with Jackson during his early coaching years, called him “a teacher, a mentor, and a friend who taught us that passion and perseverance are as important as playbooks.” Across social media, former players, broadcasters, and fans shared memories of Jackson’s signature catchphrase—“You’re welcome!”—and his ability to make even the most technical aspects of the game feel accessible.

Jackson’s death arrives at a moment when the NFL is navigating significant transitions: evolving player safety protocols, expanding international markets, and a shifting media landscape that increasingly favors streaming over traditional television. As the league looks ahead, the legacy of figures like Jackson—who bridged the gap between gritty, hard‑nosed football and modern storytelling—offers a template for future broadcasters and former players seeking to remain relevant in a digital age. His blend of authenticity, expertise, and community engagement will likely influence how the sport’s narratives are crafted for years to come.

In remembering Tom Jackson, the football world not only mourns a fierce competitor and beloved voice but also celebrates a man whose passion for the game resonated far beyond the gridiron. As the Broncos prepare for the upcoming season and ESPN continues to evolve its coverage, the imprint of Jackson’s fiery spirit will endure, reminding fans and analysts alike that the heart of football beats as much in the locker room and community centers as it does on Sunday night television.
